en.content: Two blocks, each having mass M, rest on frictionless surfaces as shown in the figure. If the pulleys are light and frictionless, and M on the incline is allowed to move down, then the tension in the string will be :
en.explanation:
Let the pulley $P_1$ be the origin.

$x_1$ is the position of the block of mass $M$ sliding down along the inclined plane of angle $\theta$, measured from the $P_1$.

$x_2$ be the horizontal position of the second block of mass $M$ moving on the horizontal ground, measured from $P_1$ along horizontal.

The block on the incline $M$ will slide down and hence the block on the horizontal ground will move to the left by same amount to keep string tight.

Thus, the total length $L$ of the inextensible string can be written as:

$$L = x_1 + x_2 + l_0$$

Differentiating this equation twice with respect to time $t$:

$$\frac{d^2 x_1}{dt^2} + \frac{d^2 x_2}{dt^2} = 0$$

Let $a_1 = \frac{d^2 x_1}{dt^2}$ be the acceleration of the inclined block down the slope, and $a_2 = -\frac{d^2 x_2}{dt^2}$ be the acceleration of the horizontal block toward the left.

$$a_1 - a_2 = 0 \Rightarrow a_2 = a_1 = a$$

For the block on the horizontal frictionless surface:

The only horizontal force acting on this block is the tension $T$ of the string pulling it forward.

$$T = Ma_2 = Ma$$

$$T = Ma \ldots (i)$$

For the block on the inclined plane:

The forces acting parallel to the incline are the component of gravity pulling it down the slope $(Mg \sin \theta)$ and the tension forces pulling it up the slope.

Applying Newton's second law along the incline:

$$Mg \sin \theta - T = Ma_1 = Ma \ldots (ii)$$

From both the equations,

$$Mg\sin\theta - T = T \Rightarrow 2T = Mg\sin\theta$$

$$\Rightarrow T = \frac{Mg\sin\theta}{2}$$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

en.content: Figure shows a wedge of mass 2 kg resting on a frictionless floor. A block of mass 1 kg is kept on the wedge and the wedge is given an acceleration of $5~\text{m/sec}^2$ towards right. Then :

options.content: the block will have an acceleration of $1~\text{m/sec}^2$ w.r.t. the wedge
net force acting on the wedge is $2~\text{N}$

en.explanation:
Mass of the block is $\mathrm{m}=1 \mathrm{~kg}$

Mass of the wedge is $\mathrm{M}=2 \mathrm{~kg}$

Acceleration of the wedge to the right is $\mathrm{a}_0=5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$

Angle of inclination of wedge with respect to horizontal is $\theta=37^{\circ}$.

When the motion of block is observed with respect to wedge then the reference frame is accelerating to the right at $a_w = 5 ext{ m/s}^2$, a pseudo-force acting on the block directed opposite to the acceleration (to the left):

$$F_{\text{pseudo}} = m \cdot a_w = 1 \times 5\text{ N} = 5\text{ N}$$

On resolving the weight and the pseudo-force into components parallel and perpendicular to the inclined surface of the wedge:

Component of weight pulling the block down the incline is

$$F_{g\parallel} = mg\sin\theta = 10\sin37^\circ = 10 \times 0.6 = 6\text{ N}$$

Component of weight pressing the block perpendicular into the incline is

$$F_{g\perp} = mg\cos\theta = 10\cos37^\circ = 10 \times 0.8 = 8\text{ N}$$

Component of pseudo force pushing the block up along the incline is

$$F_{p\parallel} = ma_w\cos\theta = 5\cos37^\circ = 5 \times 0.8 = 4\text{ N}$$

Component of pseudo force pressing the block perpendicular into the incline is

$$F_{p\perp} = ma_w\sin\theta = 5\sin37^\circ = 5 \times 0.6 = 3\text{ N}$$

In the direction perpendicular to the incline surface, the block has no motion relative to the wedge. Therefore, the upward normal reaction force $N$ balances both perpendicular components pressing into the surface:

$$N = mg\cos\theta + ma_0\sin\theta$$

$$N = 8\text{ N} + 3\text{ N} = 11\text{ N}$$

So, option (C) is correct and option (D) is incorrect.

The net force acting on the block parallel to the inclined surface:

$$F_{\text{net}\parallel} = 6\text{ N} - 4\text{ N} = 2\text{ N}\text{ (down the incline)}$$

Applying Newton's second law along the incline,

$$F_{\text{net}\parallel} = m \cdot a_{\text{rel}}$$

$$2 = 1 \times a_{\text{rel}} \Rightarrow a_{\text{rel}} = 2\text{ m/s}^2$$

So, the acceleration of block with respect to wedge is $2\text{ m/s}^2$. Hence, option (A) and (B) are incorrect.

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

en.content: A triangular block of mass M rests on a smooth surface as shown in figure. A cubical block of mass m rests on the inclined surface. If all surfaces are frictionless, the force that must be applied to M so as to keep m stationary relative to M is :
en.explanation:
To keep the smaller block m stationary relative to the wedge M , both blocks must move together horizontally as a single system with the same horizontal acceleration a.

Total mass of the system $m_t = M + m$

External horizontal force applied to the system $F_{\mathrm{ext}} = F$

Since the horizontal floor is smooth (frictionless), applying Newton's second law horizontally gives:

$$F = (M + m)a \Rightarrow a = \frac{F}{M + m} \ldots \text{(i)}$$

Assuming the reference frame of the wedge $M$, which is accelerating horizontally to the right at rate $a$, block $m$

from this frame experiences a horizontal pseudo-force directed to the left :

$$F_{\text{pseudo}} = ma$$

Component of gravity acting down the incline:

$$F_{g\parallel} = mg\sin\theta$$

Component of the pseudo-force acting up the incline:

$$F_{p\parallel} = ma\cos\theta$$

For the block $m$ to remain stationary relative to the wedge, the net force acting along the incline surface must be zero:

$$ma\cos\theta = mg\sin\theta$$

$$a\cos\theta = g\sin\theta$$

$$a = g\left(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)$$

$$a = g\tan\theta$$

$$a = g\tan 30^\circ \ldots (ii)$$

Using equation (i) and (ii),

$$F = (M + m)a$$

$$F = (M + m)g\tan 30^\circ$$

Therefore, the force required to keep the block $m$ stationary with respect to wedge is $(M + m)g\tan 30^\circ$.

Thus, the correct option is (C).

en.content: The wedge is moved towards right with acceleration $a$ which is slowly increased from zero. Find tension in the string just when the small block breaks contact with the surface of the wedge. (Assume all surfaces are smooth and string is inextensible)
en.explanation:
When observing from a reference frame accelerating to the right with an acceleration a, an object of mass m

experiences a horizontal pseudo force to the left. The magnitude of this pseudo force is ma.

On resolving the force with respect to inclined surface which is inclined at angle $\theta$ with horizontal,

Component of weight perpendicular to the incline is $F_{g\perp} = mg \cos\theta$ (into the surface)

Component of weight parallel to the incline is $F_{g\parallel} = mg \sin\theta$ (down the surface)

Component of the pseudo force ($ma$) perpendicular to inclined surface is $F_{P\perp} = ma \sin\theta$

Component of the pseudo force ($ma$) parallel to inclined surface is $F_{P\parallel} = ma \cos\theta$

The normal contact force $(N)$ is perpendicular to the surface and away from it.

For the equilibrium condition of block relative to the wedge in perpendicular direction,

$$N + ma \sin\theta = mg \cos\theta$$

$$N = mg \cos\theta - ma \sin\theta \ldots (i)$$

As the acceleration $a$ increases, the normal force $N$ decreases. At the moment the block breaks contact with the wedge surface, the normal force becomes zero $(N = 0)$:

$$0 = mg \cos\theta - ma \sin\theta$$

$$ma \sin\theta = mg \cos\theta$$

$$ma = \frac{mg\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = mg\cot\theta \Rightarrow ma = mg\cot\theta\ \ldots\ (ii)$$

For the equilibrium of block along the inclined surface,

$$T = mg\sin\theta + ma\cos\theta$$

Using equation (ii),

$$T = mg\sin\theta + \left(\frac{mg\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)\cos\theta$$

$$T = mg\sin\theta + \frac{mg\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta}$$

$$T = mg\left(\frac{\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)$$

$$T = mg\left(\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)$$

$$T = mg\,\mathrm{cosec}\theta$$

Therefore, the tension in the string when the block breaks contact is $mg\,\mathrm{cosec}\theta$. Thus, the correct option (B).

en.content: A block of mass m resting on a wedge of angle $\theta$ as shown in the figure. The wedge is given an acceleration a towards left. What is the minimum value of a due to external agent so that the mass m falls freely?
en.explanation:
For the block of mass $m$ to fall freely, it must lose contact with the inclined surface of the wedge. When an object loses contact with a surface, the normal reaction force ( N ) between the object and that surface becomes zero ( $\mathrm{N}=0$ ).

On observing the motion of block from wedge reference frame which is accelerating to the left at rate a , a horizontal pseudo-force to the block directed to the right must be exerted (opposite to the acceleration):

$$ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{pseudo}}=\mathrm{ma} $$

Gravitational force ($mg$) acting vertically downwards.

The angle between the vertical line and the normal to the incline is $\theta$. Therefore, the component pressing the block into the incline is:

$$F_{g\perp} = mg\cos\theta$$

Pseudo-force ($ma$) is acting horizontally to the right.

The angle between a horizontal line and the normal to the incline is $\theta$. Therefore, the component pulling the block away from the incline surface is:

$$F_{p\perp} = ma\sin\theta$$

The normal reaction force $N$ acting perpendicular to the incline surface satisfies the equilibrium equation:

$$N + ma\sin\theta = mg\cos\theta$$

$$N = mg\cos\theta - ma\sin\theta$$

For the block to fall freely,

$$mg\cos\theta - ma\sin\theta \leq 0$$

$$mg\cos\theta \leq ma\sin\theta$$

$$g\cos\theta \leq a\sin\theta$$

$$a \geq g \left( \frac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta} \right)$$

$$a \geq g \cot \theta$$

Thus, the minimum horizontal acceleration required for the mass to lose contact and fall freely is $a_{\min} = g \cot \theta$.

Thus, the correct option is (C).

en.content: Choose the correct equation for normal reaction $N$ between block and fixed smooth wedge, where $a$ is acceleration of block along the incline.
en.explanation:
The normal reaction force N acts perpendicular to the surface of the incline.

The normal reaction force N points outward, perpendicular to the plane.

The gravitational force mg acts vertically downward.

The angle between the vertical line and the line perpendicular to the incline is equal to the inclination angle $\theta$.

Therefore, the component of gravity acting perpendicular to the incline into the surface is $\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta$.

Along the incline the component of gravity is $\mathrm{F}_{\|}=\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta$ down the incline.

So, using Newton's second law of motion along the incline, $\mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta}{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{g} \sin \theta$

Since the wedge is fixed to the ground, the block is constrained to stay in contact with the incline and cannot accelerate or move perpendicular to its surface. Therefore, the net force in the perpendicular direction must be zero :

$$ \Sigma \mathrm{F}_{\perp}=0 $$

$$\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~N}=\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta \ldots (ii)$$

Therefore, the normal contact force is $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta$. Thus, the correct option is (B).

en.content: n blocks of different masses are placed on the frictionless inclined plane in contact. They are released at the same time. The force of interaction between (n - 1)th and nth blocks is
en.explanation:
If a block of mass $m$ placed on a frictionless inclined plane inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, the gravitational force $(mg)$ acting vertically downwards and the normal force $(N)$ acting perpendicular to the inclined surface.

Perpendicular component relative to the incline $mg\cos\theta$

Parallel component relative to the incline is $mg\sin\theta$

As there is no motion perpendicular to the inclined plane,

$$N = mg\cos\theta$$

Applying Newton's second law ($F_{\text{net}} = m \cdot a$) along the slope:

$$mg\sin\theta = ma$$

$$a = g\sin\theta$$

The acceleration down a frictionless inclined plane depends only on the angle of inclination $\theta$ and gravity $g$; it is independent of the mass of the block.

If $n$ blocks of different masses placed in contact and released at the same time.

Their individual accelerations are same, $g\sin\theta$, every block moves down the slope at the same rate.

Initial velocity of every block along the incline is $$u_1 = u_2 = u_3 = \cdots = u_n = 0$$

The acceleration of each block down the incline is $$a_1 = a_2 = a_3 = \cdots = g\sin\theta$$

At any instant of time $t$, their velocities are,

$$v_1 = u_1 + a_1 t \Rightarrow v_1 = g\sin\theta\, t$$

$$v_2 = u_2 + a_2 t \Rightarrow v_2 = g\sin\theta\, t$$

$$v_3 = u_3 + a_3 t \Rightarrow v_3 = g\sin\theta\, t$$

$$\cdots \cdots \cdots \cdots \cdots \cdots \cdots$$

$$v_n = u_n + a_n t \Rightarrow v_n = g\sin\theta\, t$$

So, every block is relatively at rest with relative to block. When two surface in contact are at rest relative to each other and also in motion, the magnitude of normal contact force is zero.

Using equation of motion for the $n^{th}$ block down the incline:

$$m_n g \, \sin \theta - N_{n,n-1} = m_n a$$

The acceleration is $a = g \sin \theta$ into the equation:

$$m_n g \, \sin \theta - N_{n,n-1} = m_n (g \sin \theta)$$

$$-N_{n,n-1} = 0 \Rightarrow N_{n,n-1} = 0$$

Thus, the force of interaction between the blocks is zero, So, the correct option is (B).

en.content: A trolley is being pulled up an inclined plane by a man sitting on it (as shown in figure). He applies a force of 250 N. If the combined mass of the man and trolley is 100 kg, the acceleration of the trolley will be [Use, $\sin 15^{\circ} = 0.26$, $g = 10 \rm{m/s^2}$]
en.explanation:
Assuming the man and the trolley together as system of mass $\mathrm{M}=100 \mathrm{~kg}$.

Let the direction up the incline as positive axis.

The total weight of the system acts vertically downwards. The component of this gravitational force acting down the incline opposing the upward motion is:

$$F_{g,\parallel} = Mg\sin\theta$$

Substituting the given values $M = 100\ \mathrm{kg}$, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $\sin 15^\circ = 0.26$:

$$F_{g,\parallel} = 100 \times 10 \times 0.26 = 260\ \mathrm{N}$$

Let $T$ be the tension in the massless rope. When the man pulls the rope with a force of $250\ \mathrm{N}$, by Newton's third law, the rope pulls back on his hands with an equal tension force, so $T = 250\ \mathrm{N}$.

One segment is held directly by the man's hands, pulling the man and therefore the system up the incline with tension $T$.

For massless pulley $P_1$ and $P_2$, the net force must be zero.

$$T_1 = T + T = 2T\ \ldots (i)$$

$$T_2 = T + T = 2T\ \ldots (ii)$$

So, the total upward force $F_{\text{upward}}$ acting on the man-trolley system is:

$$F_{\text{upward}} = T + 2T = 3T$$

$$F_{\text{upward}} = 3 \times 250\ \mathrm{N} = 750\ \mathrm{N}$$

The net force acting up the incline is:

$$F_{\text{net}} = F_{\text{upward}} - F_{g,\parallel}$$

$$F_{\text{net}} = 750\ \mathrm{N} - 260\ \mathrm{N} = 490\ \mathrm{N}$$

Using Newton's second law ($F_{\text{net}} = M \cdot a$):

$$490\ \mathrm{N} = 100a$$

$$a = \frac{490}{100}\ \mathrm{m/s^2} = 4.9\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

Therefore, the acceleration of the trolley is $4.9\ \mathrm{ms^{-2}}$. Thus, the correct option is (C).

en.content: What should be the minimum force P to be applied to the string, so that block of mass m just begins to move up the frictionless plane?
en.explanation:
The string is light (massless), so the tension T is same throughout its length and is equal to the applied pulling force $\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{P}$

On resolving the force $P$ into two components relative to the incline surface:

Component parallel to the incline is $P \cos \theta$, acting up the slope.

Component perpendicular to the incline is $P \sin \theta$, acting outward from the surface.

Therefore, the total force pulling the block-pulley system up along the inclined plane is,

$$F_{\text{upward}} = P + P \cos \theta = P(1 + \cos \theta)$$

The weight of the block acts vertically downwards with a magnitude of $Mg$.

On resolving this gravitational force into two components relative to the incline of angle $\theta$:

Component perpendicular to the incline is $Mg \cos \theta$

Component parallel to the incline $Mg \sin \theta$, which pulls the block down the slope.

For the block to just begin moving up the frictionless plane, the total upward force along the incline must balance the downward component of gravity:

$$F_{\text{upward}} = Mg \sin \theta$$

$$P(1 + \cos \theta) = Mg \sin \theta$$

$$P = \frac{Mg \sin \theta}{1 + \cos \theta}$$

Using trigonometric half-angle identities $\sin \theta = 2 \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)$; $1 + \cos \theta = 2 \cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)$

$$P = \frac{Mg \cdot 2 \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{2 \cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}$$

$$P = \frac{Mg \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}$$

$$P = Mg \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)$$

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

en.content: A man of mass $m = 60\ \text{kg}$ is standing on a weighing machine fixed on a triangular wedge of angle $\theta = 60^\circ$ as shown in the figure. The wedge is moving up with an upward acceleration $a = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$. The weight registered by machine is
en.explanation:
When a reference frame accelerates vertically upwards with an acceleration $a$, any object of mass $m$ inside that frame experiences an additional downward pseudo force equal to $ma$. This pseudo force acts in the direction opposite to the frame's acceleration.

Therefore, the total downward vertical force experienced by the man is,

$$F_{\text{downward}} = mg + ma = m(g + a)$$

An effective acceleration due to gravity ($g_{\text{eff}}$) inside the accelerating system:

$$g_{\text{eff}} = g + a$$

Using the value $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$ and the given frame acceleration $a = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$:

$$g_{\text{eff}} = 10 + 2 = 12\ \text{m/s}^2$$

The weighing machine is fixed onto the inclined surface of a triangular wedge of angle $\theta = 60^\circ$.

A weighing machine measures the normal reaction force $(N)$ pressing perpendicular to its surface.

Since the machine is parallel to the incline, the normal force it exerts on the man acts perpendicular to the inclined plane.

Component of the effective weight parallel to incline is $m g_{\mathrm{eff}} \sin \theta$, along the slope.

Component of the effective weight perpendicular to the incline is $m g_{\mathrm{eff}} \cos \theta$, into the weighing machine surface.

So, the weight registered by the weighing machine is,

$$N = m g_{\mathrm{eff}} \cos \theta$$

Substituting the given values $m = 60\ \mathrm{kg}$, $g_{\mathrm{eff}} = 12\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $\theta = 60^{\circ}$

$$N = 60 \times 12 \times \cos 60^{\circ}$$

$$N = 720 \times 0.5 = 360\ \mathrm{N}$$

Therefore, the weight registered by the machine is $360\ \mathrm{N}$. Thus, the correct option is (C).

en.content: A rod $A B$ is shown in figure. End $A$ of the rod is fixed on the ground. Block is moving with velocity $\sqrt{3} \mathbf{m} / \mathbf{s}$ towards right. What is the velocity of end $\mathbf{B}$ of rod when rod makes an angle of $\mathbf{6 0}^{\circ}$ with the ground ? (in m/s)
en.explanation:
For any rigid rod its length $L$ remains constant. Therefore, the relative velocity between its two ends along the length of the rod must be zero.

Let the fixed end $A$ be the origin $(0,0)$.

The rod has a constant length $L$.

The rod makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal ground.

The coordinates of end $B$ at any instant are given by:

$$x_B = L \cos \theta$$

$$y_B = L \sin \theta$$

As the block moves to the right, the position of every point on the block will move to the right with velocity of block $\sqrt{3}\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

Horizontal velocity component of end B is,

$$v_x = \frac{dx_B}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(L\cos\theta) = -L\sin\theta\frac{d\theta}{dt}$$

Vertical velocity component of end B is,

$$v_y = \frac{dy_B}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(L\sin\theta) = L\cos\theta\frac{d\theta}{dt}$$

As end B is in contact with the vertical face of the block moving horizontally to the right.

So, the horizontal velocity component of end B must be equal to the velocity of the block,

$$v_x = v_{\text{block}} = \sqrt{3}\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

$$\sqrt{3} = -L\sin\theta\frac{d\theta}{dt} \Rightarrow L\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\sqrt{3}\sin\theta$$

The negative sign indicates that the angle $\theta$ decreases as end B moves downward and rightward.

The vertical velocity component $v_y$ is,

$$v_y = L\cos\theta\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sin\theta}\right) = -\sqrt{3}\cot\theta$$

$$v_y = -\sqrt{3}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -1\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

The net speed $v_B$ of end B is,

$$v_B = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$$

$$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{3+1}=\sqrt{4}=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$

Therefore, the speed of end B is $2(\mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s})$.

en.content: Find the acceleration of each block. $\mathbf{1 0 0 ~ N}$ is applied horizontally.
en.explanation:
The three blocks are in contact on a smooth inclined plane with an inclination angle of $\theta=37^{\circ}$.

The masses are $\mathrm{m}_1=5 \mathrm{~kg}, \mathrm{~m}_2=3 \mathrm{~kg}, \mathrm{~m}_3=2 \mathrm{~kg}$.

A horizontal force of 100 N is applied to the block $\mathrm{m}_1$, pushing the system up the incline.

Since the blocks remain in contact and move together, they have a common acceleration a.

Considering the three blocks together as a system.

The total mass $M$ of this system:

$$M = m_1 + m_2 + m_3 = 5 kg + 3 kg + 2 kg = 10 kg$$

The total weight $Mg$ acts vertically downward. The component of this weight acting down the incline opposite to motion is:

$$F_{g,\parallel} = Mg\sin\theta$$

$$F_{g,\parallel} = 10 \times 10 \times 0.6\text{ N} = 60\text{ N}$$

The force $F = 100\text{ N}$ is pushed horizontally to the right. The component of this force along the incline is:

$$F_{\parallel} = F\cos\theta$$

$$F_{\parallel} = 100 \times 0.8\text{ N} = 80\text{ N}$$

The net force acting along the inclined plane is

$$F_{\text{net}} = F_{\parallel} - F_{g,\parallel}$$

$$F_{\text{net}} = 80\text{ N} - 60\text{ N} = 20\text{ N}$$

Using Newton's second law for the combined system ($F_{\text{net}} = M \cdot a$):

$$20\ \text{N} = 10a$$

$$a = \frac{20}{10} = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$$

Therefore, the common acceleration of each block is $2\ \text{m/s}^2$.

en.content: Find mass ( $\mathbf{M}$ ) of the hanging block, if the string in steady state makes an angle of $\mathbf{5 3}^{\circ}$ with normal to the trolley as shown in figure.
en.explanation:
Consider the 1 kg bob hanging inside the trolley. In the accelerating frame of reference of the trolley which moves up the incline with acceleration a , a horizontal pseudo force $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{b}}$ a acting downwards parallel to the incline surface due to the trolley's upward acceleration.

The downward force of gravity on bob is $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{g}=1 \times 10 \mathrm{~N}=10 \mathrm{~N}$.

The tension in string will act along the string, $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{s}}$.

On resolving these forces along incline surface, where the x -axis is parallel to the incline and the y -axis is perpendicular to the incline.

The string is making an angle of $\phi=53^{\circ}$ with the normal (y-axis).

Component along the normal (y-axis), $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{s}} \cos 53^{\circ}$

Component along the incline ( x -axis), $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{s}} \sin 53^{\circ}$

Resolving the gravitational force $\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{g}\right)$ relative to the incline making angle $37^{\circ}$ :

Component pressing normal to the surface ( y -axis), $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{g} \cos 37^{\circ}$

Component pulling down along the surface $(\mathrm{x}$-axis $), \mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{g} \sin 37^{\circ}$

Since the bob is in a steady state relative to the trolley, the net force in both directions must equal zero:

Balancing forces perpendicular to the incline ($\Sigma F_y = 0$):

$$T_s \cos 53^\circ = m_b g \cos 37^\circ \ldots \text{(i)}$$

Balancing forces parallel to the incline ($\Sigma F_x = 0$):

$$T_s \sin 53^\circ = m_b g \sin 37^\circ + m_b a \ldots \text{(ii)}$$

Dividing equation (ii) by (i)

$$\tan 53^\circ = \frac{g \sin 37^\circ + a}{g \cos 37^\circ}$$

Substituting the values $\tan 53^\circ = \frac{4}{3}$, $\sin 37^\circ = 0.6$, $\cos 37^\circ = 0.8$, and $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$:

$$\frac{4}{3} = \frac{(10 \times 0.6) + a}{10 \times 0.8}$$

$$\frac{4}{3} = \frac{6 + a}{8}$$

$$4 \times 8 = 3(6 + a)$$

$$32 = 18 + 3a \Rightarrow 3a = 14 \Rightarrow a = \frac{14}{3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

The combined mass of the trolley and the internal block is:

$$m_{\text{total}} = 5\ \mathrm{kg} + 1\ \mathrm{kg} = 6\ \mathrm{kg}$$

Let $T_c$ be the tension in the main cable connecting the trolley to the hanging block $M$.

Using the equation of motion for the trolley system moving up the incline:

$$T_c - m_{\text{total}} g \sin 37^\circ = m_{\text{total}} a$$

$$T_c = m_{\text{total}} (g \sin 37^\circ + a)$$

$$T_c = 6 \times \left(10 \times 0.6 + \frac{14}{3}\right) = 6 \times \left(6 + \frac{14}{3}\right) = 36 + 28 = 64\ \text{N}$$

The hanging block of mass $M$ moves vertically downwards with the same acceleration $a = \frac{14}{3}\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Using its equation of motion:

$$Mg - T_c = Ma$$

$$Mg - Ma = T_c \Rightarrow M(g - a) = T_c$$

Substituting $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$ and $T_c = 64\ \text{N}$:

$$M\left(10 - \frac{14}{3}\right) = 64$$

$$M\left(\frac{16}{3}\right) = 64$$

$$M = 64 \times \frac{3}{16} = 4 \times 3 = 12\ \text{kg}$$

Therefore, the mass of the hanging block is $12\ \text{kg}$.

en.content: Find the reading (in N) of spring balance as shown in figure. Assume that, mass $M$ is in equilibrium
en.explanation:
For the block of mass m = 2.5 kg on the inclined plane.

The force of gravity on block vertically down with a force equal to its weight, $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{mg}$.

$$ \mathrm{W}=2.5 \times 10 \mathrm{~N}=25 \mathrm{~N} $$

The incline surface makes an angle of $37^{\circ}$ with the horizontal.

Perpendicular component of gravity to the incline is $\mathrm{W}_{\perp}=\mathrm{mg} \cos 37^{\circ}=25 \times \frac{4}{5} \mathrm{~N}=20 \mathrm{~N}$.

Parallel component of gravity to the incline is $\mathrm{W}_{\|}=\mathrm{mg} \sin 37^{\circ}=25 \times \frac{3}{5} \mathrm{~N}=15 \mathrm{~N}$.

Since the wedge M is at rest, the net force acting on the 2.5 kg block along the direction of the incline is only due to component of its weight.

The normal force by the wedge on the block will balance the perpendicular component of gravity,

$$ \mathrm{N}=\mathrm{mg} \cos 37^{\circ}=20 \mathrm{~N} $$

On resolving the normal force along horizontal and vertical direction.

As the wedge (M) is at rest the net force acting on it will be zero.

$$ \sum \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{x}}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~F}_{\mathrm{S}}-\mathrm{N} \sin 37^{\circ}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~F}_{\mathrm{S}}=20 \times \frac{3}{5} \mathrm{~N}=12 \mathrm{~N} $$

The reading of spring balance is equal to the horizontal component of normal contact force between m and M , i.e., 12 N.

en.content: A block of mass 1 kg is kept on the tilted floor of a lift moving down with $3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. If the block is released from rest as shown, what will be the time (in s) taken by block to reach the bottom?
en.explanation:
The lift is moving vertically downwards with an acceleration $\mathrm{a}_0=3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$.

When observing motion from an accelerating frame of reference, we apply a pseudo force in the opposite direction of the frame's acceleration.

Since the frame accelerates downwards, the pseudo force acts vertically upwards with a magnitude of $\mathrm{ma}_0$.

An effective acceleration due to gravity ( $\mathrm{g}_{\text {eff }}$ ) from the frame of lift is,

$$ \mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathrm{g}-\mathrm{a}_0 $$

Taking $\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ and $\mathrm{a} \_0=3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ :

$$ \mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{eff}}=10-3=7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 $$

The tilted floor is inclined with an angle of $\theta = 37^\circ$ relative to the horizontal.

The effective weight of the block inside the lift is $m\,g_{\mathrm{eff}}$, acting vertically downwards.

On resolving the forces relative to the incline surface:

The component perpendicular to the tilted floor is $m\,g_{\mathrm{eff}}\cos 37^\circ$ towards surface.

The component parallel down the slope is $m\,g_{\mathrm{eff}}\sin 37^\circ$

Since the floor is frictionless, the only unbalanced force on the block along the incline is the parallel component of gravity.

Using Newton's second law along the incline ($F_{\mathrm{net}} = m a_{\mathrm{rel}}$):

$$m\,g_{\mathrm{eff}}\sin 37^\circ = m\,a_{\mathrm{rel}}$$

$$a_{\mathrm{rel}} = g_{\mathrm{eff}}\sin 37^\circ$$

$$a_{\mathrm{rel}} = 7 \times 0.6 = 4.2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

The block is released from rest, so its initial velocity relative to the floor is $u = 0$.

The length of the tilted floor it must traverse to reach the bottom is $s = 2.1\ \mathrm{m}$.

Using the kinematic equation of motion ($s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$):

$$2.1 = 0 \times t + \frac{1}{2} \times (4.2) \times t^2$$

$$2.1 = 2.1\,t^2$$

$$t^2 = 1 \Rightarrow t = 1\ \mathrm{s}$$

Therefore, the time taken by the block to reach the bottom is $1\ \mathrm{s}$.
